question: The scope note for the class covering transfer of custody of museum objects was found to contain an internal contradiction about whether it always covered physical possession. Was a fix accepted, and what was the reasoning behind it?
gold_answer: Yes, the fix was accepted. The original wording described the class as being about transfer of physical custody, but a later paragraph in the same note allowed for transfers of only legal custody, contradicting the opening line. The proposed fix redefined the class to cover transfer of physical custody or of legal responsibility for custody, with the specific case (physical-only, legal-only, or both) to be expressed separately using the P2 has type property rather than being baked into the base definition. The e-vote passed with every respondent voting yes, several attaching minor editorial caveats (a missing verb, punctuation, and a request to clarify the examples), and those caveats were folded into a revised note read out at the following SIG meeting.
key_facts: The e-vote to revise the Transfer of Custody scope note passed with unanimous yes votes, some with minor wording caveats
The fix redefined the class to cover transfer of physical custody or of legal responsibility for custody, rather than physical custody alone
The distinction between a physical-only, legal-only, or combined transfer is meant to be expressed using the P2 has type property, not stated directly in the base scope note
produced_answer: Yes, a fix was accepted. Robert Sanderson raised NEW ISSUE 475 on 2020-02-18 (thread t1325), pointing out that the E10 Transfer of Custody scope note contradicted itself: its first line said the class comprises 'transfers of physical custody of objects,' but a later paragraph implied a transfer could be of legal responsibility only, distinguished via P2 has type. He asked how legal-but-not-physical custody (e.g. an eBay sale, a pending house sale, an auction house that may only hold a photograph) could be modeled if E10 was strictly physical. As homework from SIG 47 (thread t1375, 2020-06-25), Sanderson drafted a fix: the first sentence should say the class comprises transfers of EITHER the physical custody OR the legal responsibility for physical custody, and the P2-has-type sentence should be reworded to say that when only ONE kind (legal OR physical, not both) is being documented, that distinction is expressed via P2 has type -- rather than implying physical was always the default. This went to an e-vote (thread t1394, Oct 2020, subject 'E-Vote: Change of Scope Note E10 Transfer of Custody (Issue 475)'). Sanderson's cover message explicitly named the reasoning: 'the scope note seemed to contain a contradiction since the first line indicated that the transfer of custody was of physical possession while the second paragraph indicated that it could be of physical possession OR only of legal custody,' and the fix would 'consistently express that the base line case is that BOTH physical and legal custody are transferred and in the case that it is only one or the other this would be expressed using the p2 has type property.' The vote passed unanimously YES (Sanderson, Martin Doerr, van Leusen, Oyvind Eide, Christian-Emil Ore, Pat Riva), with several voters attaching editorial caveats (missing verb, clearer wording on 'representative part' for physical possession, examples to be reviewed). George Bruseker incorporated these caveats into a revised scope note (2020-10-18) reading 'This class comprises transfers of the physical custody or the legal responsibility for the physical custody of objects,' with the P2-has-type sentence fixed to 'In the event that only a single kind of transfer of custody occurs, either the legal responsibility for the custody or the actual physical possession of the object but not both, this difference should be expressed using the property P2 has type.' The current ontology entry (search.py concept E10, v7.1.3) contains exactly this wording, and the episode for Issue 475 is marked [decided], confirming the fix was adopted as proposed.

question: In CRMarchaeo, how did the classification of an 'embedding' (a physical thing being buried or set within surrounding matter) change, and what follow-on property problem did that change create?
gold_answer: The SIG decided to reclassify embedding from a subclass of a generic condition-state class to a subclass of the Rigid Physical Feature class, following a proposal that the surrounding matter is itself often what is used to infer things like the time of deposition; this was backed despite an objection that embedding felt more immaterial than a physical feature and better suited to the condition-state framing. Once reclassified this way, the class's own temporal-bounds aspect effectively disappeared, since a Rigid Physical Feature's genesis event was expected to carry that information instead. That change then created a follow-on problem: the property linking an embedding to the stratigraphic unit that contains it was still restricted to a single kind of stratigraphic volume, but many excavation records only record embeddings loosely, without distinguishing an actual layer from a stratigraphic interface. One member proposed broadening that property's range to the shared parent class covering both, but this drew an objection that letting an embedding be 'in' an interface is conceptually odd since an interface is essentially two-dimensional; the counter-argument, using examples like a mass grave with bones embedded across multiple layers, was that embeddings spanning several layers and interfaces are real and should be representable, and by the end of the exchange the proposer of the range change had come around to supporting the broader range.
key_facts: The SIG decided to make the embedding class a subclass of the Rigid Physical Feature class rather than keeping it under the generic condition-state class
This reclassification removed the class's own explicit temporal-bounds handling, since a Rigid Physical Feature's genesis event was expected to cover timing instead

The reclassification triggered a debate over widening the range of the 'is embedding in' property from a specific stratigraphic-layer class to the broader stratigraphic-unit class covering both layers and interfaces, to match how excavators often record finds without distinguishing the two

The objection to the broader range was that an embedding being 'in' an interface is conceptually odd because an interface is essentially two-dimensional; this was countered with real examples of embeddings spanning multiple layers
produced_answer: In CRMarchaeo, A7 Embedding (the state/feature of a physical thing being partially or completely embedded within surrounding matter of an A2 Stratigraphic Volume Unit) was originally classified as a temporal State/Condition (a subclass of S16 State in 2016, later E3 Condition State by 2021). Issue 447 ('A7 Embedding as Rigid Physical Feature', discussed Feb-Mar 2021 and decided at the 49th joint SIG/ISO meeting) reclassified A7 Embedding as a subclass of S20 Rigid Physical Feature instead. Gerald Hiebel argued for this because the surrounding matter's condition is used to infer deposition time; Martin Doerr supported it, noting a Rigid Physical Feature's genesis event already supplies the temporal information, so a separate temporal property is unnecessary. Christian-Emil Ore noted this reclassification made the earlier temporal aspect of A7 disappear, and Achille Felicetti objected that an embedding is 'something more immaterial' than a physical feature. The reclassification created a follow-on property problem for AP19 'is embedding in (contains embedding)', whose range was fixed to A2 Stratigraphic Volume Unit. Because many excavations record structures without distinguishing layers (A2) from surfaces/interfaces (A3), and because a physical-feature embedding (per Martin Doerr's Talheim Death Pit / multi-layer examples) can span multiple stratigraphic units, Christian-Emil Ore proposed (thread t1445, March 2021) widening AP19's range from A2 to A8 (the common superclass of A2 and A3). Achille Felicetti flagged this as formally fine but conceptually disputable: it would license triples stating an A7 Embedding 'is embedding in' an A3 Stratigraphic Interface, even though an interface is a 2D feature things cannot literally be embedded within. This range/property issue was left unresolved in the archive -- the concept chronology for A7 marks the Issue 447 classification change and the AP19-range discussion both as 'unresolved'.

question: A modeller proposed a strict rule that any 'mark' applied to an object which is not also an inscription can never be treated as encoding actual language. Was that rule adopted, and separately, how was the disputed clause about the intent behind marks (indicating a creator, owner, dedication, etc.) eventually reworded?
gold_answer: The strict rule was rejected. It was pointed out that just because inscriptions (marks known to carry language) are a subset of marks does not license the reverse closed-world claim that no other marks could also happen to carry language — doing so would conflict with the open-world assumption the model is built on. Other proposed relationships in the same discussion, such as marks being a kind of symbolic/information object and inscriptions being the subset of marks that are also linguistic objects, were accepted as correct. Separately, the scope note's language about intent was reworded after members objected that examples like a casual graffito or a warning sign didn't fit a definition requiring intent to indicate a creator, owner, dedication, or purpose. The fix loosened that clause from a defining condition into an illustration of typical use, ending up with wording to the effect that marks are applied 'often' to indicate such things, or more generally just to communicate information.
key_facts: The proposed rule that non-inscription marks can never be linguistic objects was rejected as an inappropriate closed-world assumption
Other proposed class relationships from the same discussion (marks as symbolic/information objects, inscriptions as the linguistic-object subset of marks) were accepted as correct

The scope note's intent clause was reworded from a defining condition into an illustrative one, using wording like marks being applied 'often' to indicate a creator, owner, dedication or purpose, or more generally to communicate information
produced_answer: The strict rule was NOT adopted. In the E37 Mark scope-note discussion (thread t1300, Issue 463, Jan-Jun 2020), Robert Sanderson listed five inheritance assertions (A-E), with E being 'No Marks which are not also Inscriptions are Linguistic Objects.' Ethan Gruber disagreed with E, citing mint marks like the letter 'P' on American coins (obviously linguistic but not necessarily classed as Inscriptions). Martin Doerr also explicitly rejected E, arguing it 'violates the Open World assumption' -- CRM knows Inscriptions are Linguistic Objects but that does not imply no OTHER Marks can be Linguistic Objects too -- and said he saw 'no particular utility in this statement,' while affirming 'All other rules A-D provided by Robert appear to be correct.' So the strict exclusion rule was dropped/rejected, not adopted. Separately, the disputed intent clause was reworded: the old scope note said marks are applied 'in order to indicate the creator, owner, dedications, purpose, etc.' (a phrasing Robert Sanderson objected to as implying ALL marks/inscriptions must carry that intent, citing counterexamples like 'Kilroy was here' and the Balliol 'Keep off the grass' sign). Martin Doerr's final revision (2020-06-11) changed this to a non-restrictive, illustrative clause: marks are applied 'by arbitrary techniques, often in order to indicate such things as creator, owner, dedications, purpose or to communicate information generally' -- adding the qualifier 'often' and 'such things as' so it reads as typical use rather than a defining restriction. This matches the current published E37 Mark scope note in the ontology.

question: The community discussed extending the CRM so that non-human animals (for example, a bird building a nest) could be documented as having carried out an activity, the way a human actor would. Did the SIG settle on a new class structure for this, and if not, what was left unresolved?
gold_answer: No, the SIG did not settle on or adopt any new class structure for non-human actors, despite substantial discussion. The case was raised using the example of a bird (or dinosaur) building a nest, for which the model had no adequate way to assign agency short of a weak 'occurred in the presence of' relation. Two members sketched a detailed proposal for a monotonic extension, introducing a sibling superclass to the human-actor class with parallel individual and collective biological-agent subclasses, and suggested eventually renaming the existing human-specific classes accordingly. However, another member consistently held that any such extension needed an established community documentation practice and willing domain experts first, neither of which existed yet, and separately drew a firm line that machines or robots should never count as actors regardless of their apparent agency, since they act on behalf of human instructions much like a trap does. A librarian on the list added that an analogous 'animal as agent' idea had already been proposed and rejected in the bibliographic (FRBR/LRM) community for similar reasons. The discussion ended with a proposal to document the debate itself as methodological material and the sharing of a real-world animal-tracking use case, but no class or property was ever adopted.
key_facts: No new class or property for non-human actors was adopted; the discussion ended without the SIG reaching a decision
A detailed extension proposal was put forward (a sibling agent superclass with individual/collective biological-agent subclasses, and renaming existing human-actor classes), but it was not adopted

One member's stated position was that such an extension requires an established documentation practice and domain experts first, which the group had not yet found, and that machines/robots should never count as actors
A librarian noted that an analogous animal-as-agent proposal had already been considered and rejected in the FRBR/LRM bibliographic model for similar reasons
produced_answer: No, the SIG did not settle on a new class structure. The thread 'New Issue: Non-human Actors' (started by Robert Sanderson, Sept 2021, using the bird-nest example) produced a detailed proposal from George Bruseker/Rob Sanderson for a new sibling hierarchy to E39 Actor (a general 'Agent' superclass splitting into Individual Agent/Collective Agent, with Biological Agent siblings to the human-only branch, and E39/E21/E74 renamed to 'Human' variants). Martin Doerr did not accept this as a starting point: he argued CRM methodology requires starting from concrete use-case properties and domain-expert input rather than positing a class top-down, and that the bird-nest case is better handled (if at all) via a new 'S17 Physical Genesis' subclass ('Biological Genesis') with a property like 'done by species' (E55 Type) rather than a full non-human Actor/Agent class - individual-animal agency was, in his view, a much weaker and unresolved case. Left unresolved by the end of the thread (last substantive message Nov 2021, later message just shares background slides): (1) whether any new class is needed at all, versus using P12 'occurred in the presence of' plus type-level description; (2) the scope of any such extension - animals only, or also plants/bacteria/machines (Doerr argued machines/robots should be a separate 'reaction' category, not agents); (3) how to handle individual vs. species/type-level identity for animals, given the lack of a stable cross-domain concept of animal individuality; and (4) the need for domain experts (biologists) and real use-case data, which the SIG felt it still lacked. Rob Sanderson noted the group would take the sketched proposal to Linked.Art instead, pending any future SIG resolution. The archive's own concept chronology for E39 Actor tags this thread as 'unresolved'.

question: The CIDOC CRM introduction has a passage about properties whose domain and range are the same class, discussing when such properties are symmetric versus transitive. This passage was flagged as flawed and eventually revised. What was wrong with the original wording, and how was it finally changed?
gold_answer: The original bullet under Naming Conventions claimed that properties with identical domain and range are 'either symmetric or transitive', which is both a false dichotomy and, once corrected, still redundant with material already covered elsewhere. A reviewer pointed out the counterexample P152 has parent (is parent of), which has identical domain and range but is neither symmetric nor transitive. After discussion, the SIG agreed the paragraph was trying to restate concepts (symmetry, transitivity, reflexivity) that are already defined precisely in the Terminology section, and that the only thing actually relevant to Naming Conventions is that symmetric properties get no parenthetical inverse label. The text was trimmed down to just that point, illustrated with P122 borders with (E53 Place), with a pointer back to the Terminology section's definition of 'symmetric'. This shortened wording was put to an e-vote (issue 686) in March 2025 and passed unanimously, to be adopted in CIDOC CRM v7.3.
key_facts: The original text wrongly asserted that identical-domain/range properties are 'either symmetric or transitive', disproved by the counterexample P152 has parent (is parent of), which is neither.

The agreed fix removed the redundant discussion of transitivity/reflexivity from Naming Conventions (already covered in the Terminology section) and kept only the point that symmetric properties (e.g. P122 borders with) have no parenthetical inverse label.
The revised wording was passed by unanimous e-vote (issue 686) in March 2025 for adoption in CIDOC CRM v7.3.
produced_answer: The passage is the bullet point under 'Naming Conventions' in the CRMbase introduction. The original (v7.3-current) wording read: "Properties that have identical domain and range are either symmetric or transitive. Instantiating a symmetric property implies that the same relation holds for both the domain-to-range and the range-to-domain directions. An example of this is E53 Place. P122 borders with: E53 Place. The names of symmetric properties have no parenthetical form, because reading in the range-to-domain direction is the same as the domain-to-range reading. Transitive asymmetric properties, such as E4 Period. P9 consists of (forms part of): E4 Period, have a parenthetical form that relates to the meaning of the inverse direction." Wolfgang Schmidle flagged it (thread t1797, Oct 2024) as needing reformulation. Christian-Emil Smith Ore pointed out the actual flaw: having identical domain and range is NOT a sufficient condition for a property to be symmetric or transitive (counter-example: P152 has parent (is parent of) has identical domain/range but is neither symmetric nor transitive), and the opening sentence 'Properties that have identical domain and range are either symmetric or transitive' is simply false as stated (an even 'fixed' version, 'either symmetric, asymmetric, or neither', was noted as a tautology). Martin Doerr argued the whole paragraph was redundant patching, since symmetry/transitivity/reflexivity are already properly defined in the Terminology section, and repeating them under Naming Conventions only creates a maintenance pitfall (as just happened). He proposed shortening it to just the point actually relevant to naming conventions: the fact that symmetric properties have no parenthetical form. This was formalized as issue 686 and put to an E-VOTE in March 2025 (thread t1817), which passed unanimously (Wolfgang Schmidle, Martin Doerr, Christian-Emil implicitly, Oyvind Eide, Pat Riva, Athanasios Velios all voted YES). The final replacement text (adopted for CIDOC CRM v7.3+) is: "The names of symmetric properties have no parenthetical form, because reading in the range-to-domain direction is the same as the domain-to-range reading. An example of this is E53 Place. P122 borders with: E53 Place. See the definition of 'symmetric' in the section 'Terminology'." The reference to transitive/asymmetric properties (e.g. E4 Period. P9 consists of (forms part of): E4 Period) was dropped entirely as redundant with the Terminology section.

question: Within CIDOC CRM, is it valid to infer that if an event took place at a place Y, and place Y falls within a larger place Z, then the event also took place at Z? What did the CRM-SIG conclude about this, and what reasoning came up around it?
gold_answer: No, this chained inference is not treated as valid. The SIG had already decided, per homework prepared for issue 606, that the rule combining 'took place at' with the containment property for places should not appear in the formal logic, and Martin Doerr argued it had never been ontologically sound in the first place rather than merely inconvenient: it conflated an 'inverse shortcut' with an ordinary shortcut, and mechanically closing the location property under the entire containment hierarchy above an attested place would flood a knowledge base with unbounded, unhelpful derived statements. The intended reading is that the location property should express the narrowest reasonable outer approximation of where something happened (illustrated with Caesar's murder being narrowed from Rome to the Forum Romanum to a specific building), not an arbitrarily wide one produced by walking up the containment chain. In the ensuing exchange, Wolfgang Schmidle argued a restricted version of widening is still needed — via the intersection of multiple attested locations for the same event, using a proposed 'overlap' function — mainly to detect contradictions between differing attestations rather than to derive new, previously-unknown locations; the discussion did not converge on a single revised formal rule to replace the removed one.
key_facts: The SIG had already decided, in homework for issue 606, that the location-property/containment-chaining inference does not hold, and Martin Doerr stated it was never true rather than newly disallowed.

The stated rationale is that closing the location property under the full containment hierarchy would generate unbounded, unhelpful derived statements, and conflates an inverse shortcut with a genuine shortcut.

The location property is meant to express the narrowest reasonable outer approximation of where something happened (illustrated by narrowing Caesar's murder from Rome to the Forum Romanum to a specific building), not the widest possible containing place.

Wolfgang Schmidle argued a restricted form is still needed, via the intersection of multiple attested locations for an event, mainly to catch contradictions between attestations rather than to derive new ones, and the thread ends without the SIG settling on a replacement formal rule.
produced_answer:
No. CRM-SIG explicitly rejected the naive transitive-closure inference P7(x,y) ∧ P89(y,z) ⇒ P7(x,z) (event x took place at y, y falls within z, therefore x took place at z). This was raised as Issue 617 (also discussed as part of Issue 606, and reflected later in Issue 656). Christian-Emil Ore's Issue 617 email (2022-11-28, thread t1675) reports the decision from the Rome SIG meeting: 'The answer to the question is that P7(x,y) ∧ P89(y,z) ⇒ P7(x,z) is in general not considered true. This axiom has to be reintroduced if this is the general understanding. It is not needed in practical database/KB implementations.' Instead of upward closure over P89 containment, P7 was reformulated to imply only the 'fully developed path' from E4 Period through P161 has spatial projection to E53 Place, P89 falls within to E53 Place, where both places are defined in the same geometric/reference system — i.e. the period's spatial projection is P89-contained, not that every larger place enclosing an attested P7 place automatically becomes a new P7 place. This exact wording ended up in the current (v7.1.3) scope notes of P7 and P89 (confirmed via `search.py concept P7`/`concept P89`), and was further refined editorially in Issue 656 (2024, thread t1759).

Reasoning that came up in thread t1637 ('Is P7(x,y) ∧ P89(y,z) ⇒ P7(x,z) still regarded as true?'): Martin Doerr argued the axiom 'was never true' and that the oral SIG rationale ('causes a useless recursion through the world') was really pointing at a deeper confusion — mistaking an inverse shortcut for a shortcut. He held that P7 should express a reasonable, NOT arbitrarily large, outer approximation of where something happened (narrower is better), and that the useful operation on multiple attested P7 places is their intersection (best approximation, and a way to detect inconsistencies between sources), not their union or upward propagation. Christian-Emil separately gave a practical/implementation argument (from the Issue 606 homework): letting systems chase the P89 containment graph to deduce ever-larger P7 statements would flood real KBs with true-but-useless facts, comparable to inferring a historical event happened 'in the 14th century' from a tighter date range — technically valid but not how historians actually reason. Wolfgang Schmidle pushed on this at length, distinguishing what he called S1 (P7 implies its P161 spatial projection falls within the attested P7 place) from S2 (any place between the phenomenal place and an attested P7 also counts as P7), showing S2's licensed set of places is oddly shaped (not even the union of attested places) and of dubious practical use; he proposed instead a function symbol F121 'overlap of' to formalize the useful intersection operation. The SIG's settled position was to keep S1-style containment (via P161/P89) but drop S2-style upward inference of new P7 facts.

question: CIDOC CRM's class for physical human-made things gives a sword as an example, even though a sword is really an instance of the more specific movable-object subclass, not the immovable-feature subclass that shares the same parent. How did the SIG explain why a superclass's scope note can cite subclass-level examples like this, and what specific gap about movability did the discussion turn up?
gold_answer: The SIG explained that CRM deliberately uses subclass-level examples (a sword for the movable-object subclass, rock art for the feature subclass) when writing a superclass's scope note, because otherwise users tend to misread the superclass as some kind of leftover category rather than as the generalization that actually includes its subclasses' instances; this is a known didactic tradeoff, and the SIG agreed it would help to name the responsible subclass in parentheses next to each example. The deeper issue the discussion surfaced is that this superclass itself says nothing about movability: only the class for physical objects with well-defined, separable boundaries (and its adequate subclasses) can properly be the target of a Move event, while human-made features generally cannot be moved independently of what they are attached to. To close that gap, Martin Doerr proposed adding text making explicit that Move applies only to that physical-object class or suitable subclasses, that a permanently attached item can still count as such an object if it could in principle be detached along its original boundaries, and that moving something whose boundaries must be redefined (his example was relocating the Temple of Abu Simbel) instead creates a new physical-object instance via a transformation event. This was opened as a fresh issue about movability in scope notes rather than settled by a vote within the thread.
key_facts: The shared superclass (E24) covers both the movable-object subclass (E22, exemplified by a sword) and the generally-immovable feature subclass (E25, exemplified by rock art); citing subclass-level examples in a superclass's scope note is intentional CRM pedagogy, and the SIG agreed naming the responsible subclass in parentheses would reduce confusion.
Only E18 Physical Object (and its adequate subclasses) can be the target of E9 Move; the superclass E24 by itself carries no movability information.

Martin Doerr proposed new scope-note text stating a permanently attached item can still count as E18 if it could in principle be detached along its original boundaries, and that a move requiring newly-defined boundaries (e.g. the Temple of Abu Simbel) instead produces a new E18 instance via E81 Transformation.
This was raised as a new issue on scope notes about movability; no vote or final text was recorded within the thread.
produced_answer: In the Dec 2025 thread "[Crm-sig] E24 Physical Human-Made Thing" (t1874), Dominic Oldman questioned E24's scope note, which uses a sword as an example even though a sword is really an E22 Man-Made Object, not an E25 Man-Made Feature. Christian-Emil Ore noted this is not the only scope note where a superclass example is really a subclass instance, and wondered if the 'no explicit subclass reference' rule is more an ideal than a followed practice. Martin Doerr then explained the SIG's rationale directly: they "deliberately decided to use instances of subclasses as examples, because it is the only way to make people aware what a superclass is. Otherwise, they typically regard it as a complement of the subclasses" -- citing the recurring question "what is the difference between a physical thing and a physical object?" as the problem this practice is meant to prevent. He added that if the E-number of the most adequate subclass isn't given in parentheses next to the example, that should be corrected. On movability specifically, the discussion surfaced a real gap: neither E18 Physical Object's nor E24's scope notes said anything about which classes can actually be moved. Doerr proposed adding to E18's scope note that many instances of physical-thing classes 'cannot be moved as a whole independently from surrounding or attached matter... Therefore, the class E9 Move applies only to adequate subclasses as targets of a move' (using the Temple of Abu Simbel before its transfer as the example of an unmovable-as-is instance). He also proposed clarifying that an item permanently attached/incorporated into another object may still count as an E18 Physical Object if it could in principle be detached along its original natural boundaries, but that if moving requires cutting new boundaries (again, Abu Simbel), a new E18 instance is created instead, documented via E81 Transformation. The email subject line was updated to '... NEW ISSUE scope notes on movability', indicating this gap was spun off as a new SIG issue.

question: CIDOC CRM's RDF implementation has long included a combined class for a name that is also treated as an expression in a particular language (formed by multiple inheritance from the classes for linguistic objects and for appellations), but this class exists only in the RDF files, without a documented scope note in the base standard. Did the SIG ever agree to formally add this class, with a proper scope note, to the standard itself?
gold_answer: No, and the archive never settles this. A 2022 thread pointed out that the RDF-only class for a name-that-is-also-a-linguistic-expression is inconsistently labelled and has no documentation outside the RDFS file, and proposed promoting it to a fully specified class in CRMbase. This produced an extended and ultimately unresolved debate: Martin Doerr held that CRM's minimality principle bars adding classes that contribute nothing beyond what multiple inheritance already implies, and repeatedly asked for a scope note and disambiguating examples showing that 'the language of a name' is a well-defined, non-arbitrary notion, raising counterexamples about transliterated and multi-language names that were never fully answered. Robert Sanderson and George Bruseker countered that the class is ubiquitously used in practice and that the minimality principle is already applied inconsistently to other classes (their example was E27 Site), so it should simply be documented rather than left informal. Francesco Beretta proposed reframing the concept instead as a kind of 'appellation in a language' activity/state class, which Rob argued did not meet the original requirement. The discussion carried into a formal issue at the following SIG meeting, but by the last messages in this exchange Martin was still preparing the disambiguating examples he considered necessary, and no scope note, wording, or vote had been agreed.
key_facts: The disputed class is the RDF-only combined class for a name expressed in a language (linked via the property for language of expression), which has no scope note or agreed single name in the base CRM standard, only inconsistent labels in the RDFS file.

Martin Doerr's objection rests on CRM's minimality principle (no class from multiple inheritance alone without its own distinguishing properties), and his repeated request for disambiguating examples of 'the language of a name' was never resolved.

Robert Sanderson and George Bruseker argued the class is already in wide practical use and that the minimality principle is applied inconsistently elsewhere (their counterexample was E27 Site), so it should be documented rather than left informal.

Francesco Beretta's alternative proposal to model it as an 'appellation in a language' activity/state class was rejected by Rob as not meeting the stated requirement, and the thread ends with no scope note, wording, or vote agreed.
produced_answer: No. The class is E33_E41_Linguistic_Appellation (multiple-inherits from E33 Linguistic Object and E41 Appellation), and George Bruseker raised exactly this problem in Nov 2022 ('error in RDFS for 7.1.1...'), arguing it should be a full documented class rather than an RDFS-only construct. This became Issue 624 ('Add E33_E41_Linguistic_Appellation to the Official Specification'). Robert Sanderson and George pushed for adding it with a scope note; Martin Doerr and Pavlos Fafalios pushed back, citing the CRM minimality principle (no class without properties distinctly its own) and demanding disambiguating examples before any scope note could be written. Alternative proposals (Francesco Beretta's sdh:C11 'Appellation in a Language', a new property 'E41 is used in E56 Language', LRM Nomen) were floated as substitutes but were themselves contested (Robert Sanderson said they didn't meet the requirement that the Appellation itself carry the language). By the last message found (19 Dec 2022, Athanasios Velios), the issue was still open, with Martin Doerr saying he was still working on a disambiguating example. No e-vote, scope note, or closure of Issue 624 appears anywhere in the archive through the most recent threads searched (into 2025/early 2026), and the search tool's own episode chronology for E41 marks both relevant episodes (t1649, t1682) as 'unresolved' with no later 'decided' entry for this topic. So the SIG discussed and never agreed to formally add this class to the base standard; it remains RDF-only.
